questions.q: According to Austin Kleon, where does your own style come from?
a: The places where you fail to copy your idols exactly
The moment you invent something nobody has tried
The techniques you learn in formal art school
The praise you receive from critics and fans
questions.why: Lesson 1 says the gaps left when imitation breaks down are where your unique way of working appears.

questions.q: What kind of copying does the summary call the bad kind?
a: Putting your name on someone else’s work
Following a tutorial step by step
Imitating an artist you admire
Rebuilding a project that already exists
questions.why: Lesson 1 contrasts plagiarism, illustrated by the German minister’s thesis scandal, with imitation for learning.

questions.q: Why can procrastination be productive for an artist?
a: Insights surface when you let your mind wander during downtime
It keeps you from comparing yourself with others
It forces you to work faster when you return
It proves that you are not taking the work too seriously
questions.why: Lesson 2 says flashes of insight arrive during downtime, so it should be part of the routine.

questions.q: What does the summary advise about hobbies and side projects?
a: Keep them, because diverse inputs make your output more creative
Drop them so you can focus entirely on your art
Replace them with more time at your desk
Only keep the ones that earn money
questions.why: Lesson 2 says hobbies, chores and even idle video watching feed new ideas into your creative work.

questions.q: What is the advantage of being anonymous as a beginner?
a: You are free to experiment and fail without scrutiny
You can charge higher prices for your work
People assume you are more experienced than you are
You avoid the pressure of finding an audience later
questions.why: Lesson 3 says obscurity lets you run weird experiments and make mistakes without anyone judging.
